claim: The pedal ganglion contains the pattern generator for Aplysia locomotion.
source: The pedal ganglion presents an ideal target for testing hypotheses of movement control as it contains the pattern generator (Jahan-Parwar and Fredman, 1979, 1980), motorneurons (Hening et al., 1979; Fredman and Jahan-Parwar, 1980) and modulatory neurons (Hall and Lloyd, 1990; McPherson and Blankenship, 1992) underlying locomotion.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work establishing the pedal ganglion's role in locomotion pattern generation.

claim: The pedal ganglion contains motorneurons underlying locomotion.
source: The pedal ganglion presents an ideal target for testing hypotheses of movement control as it contains the pattern generator (Jahan-Parwar and Fredman, 1979, 1980), motorneurons (Hening et al., 1979; Fredman and Jahan-Parwar, 1980) and modulatory neurons (Hall and Lloyd, 1990; McPherson and Blankenship, 1992) underlying locomotion.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work identifying motorneurons in the pedal ganglion.

claim: The pedal ganglion contains modulatory neurons underlying locomotion.
source: The pedal ganglion presents an ideal target for testing hypotheses of movement control as it contains the pattern generator (Jahan-Parwar and Fredman, 1979, 1980), motorneurons (Hening et al., 1979; Fredman and Jahan-Parwar, 1980) and modulatory neurons (Hall and Lloyd, 1990; McPherson and Blankenship, 1992) underlying locomotion.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work identifying modulatory neurons in the pedal ganglion.

claim: Fictive locomotion in the pedal ganglion is sustained for minutes.
source: Moreover, its fictive locomotion is sustained for minutes, ideal for robustly characterising population dynamics.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental system's properties based on the authors' observations.

claim: The joint activity of neural populations is high dimensional and complex.
source: The joint activity of neural populations is high dimensional and complex.
evidence: This is a general statement about neural population activity supported by the literature context provided.

claim: Population recordings have as many dimensions as neurons.
source: Population recordings have as many dimensions as neurons, and each neuron's activity can have a complex form.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about the dimensionality of population recordings.

claim: Low-dimensional signals have been described in neural circuits for sensory encoding.
source: Such low-dimensional signals within joint population activity have been described in neural circuits for sensory encoding (Mazor and Laurent, 2005; Bartho et al., 2009), decision-making (Briggman et al., 2005; Harvey et al., 2012; Mante et al., 2013), navigation (Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015; Peyrache et al., 2015), and movement (Levi et al., 2005; Ahrens et al., 2012; Kato et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on sensory encoding circuits.

claim: Low-dimensional signals have been described in neural circuits for decision-making.
source: Such low-dimensional signals within joint population activity have been described in neural circuits for sensory encoding (Mazor and Laurent, 2005; Bartho et al., 2009), decision-making (Briggman et al., 2005; Harvey et al., 2012; Mante et al., 2013), navigation (Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015; Peyrache et al., 2015), and movement (Levi et al., 2005; Ahrens et al., 2012; Kato et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on decision-making circuits.

claim: Low-dimensional signals have been described in neural circuits for navigation.
source: Such low-dimensional signals within joint population activity have been described in neural circuits for sensory encoding (Mazor and Laurent, 2005; Bartho et al., 2009), decision-making (Briggman et al., 2005; Harvey et al., 2012; Mante et al., 2013), navigation (Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015; Peyrache et al., 2015), and movement (Levi et al., 2005; Ahrens et al., 2012; Kato et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on navigation circuits.

claim: Low-dimensional signals have been described in neural circuits for movement.
source: Such low-dimensional signals within joint population activity have been described in neural circuits for sensory encoding (Mazor and Laurent, 2005; Bartho et al., 2009), decision-making (Briggman et al., 2005; Harvey et al., 2012; Mante et al., 2013), navigation (Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015; Peyrache et al., 2015), and movement (Levi et al., 2005; Ahrens et al., 2012; Kato et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on movement circuits.

claim: Three escape locomotion bouts were evoked in each preparation by stimulation of tail nerve Pd9.
source: Three escape locomotion bouts were evoked in each preparation by stimulation of tail nerve Pd9.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The population firing rate decays slowly post-stimulus.
source: But the variety of single neuron dynamics (Bruno et al., 2015) (Figure 1C) and the slowly decaying population firing rate (Figure 1F) post-stimulus hint at a more complex underlying dynamical system driving locomotion than a simple, consistent oscillator.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1E (labeled as 1F in text).

claim: Stimulation caused a strong deviation from the spontaneous state, which then settled into repeated loops.
source: Projections of a population's joint activity into three dimensions typically showed that stimulation caused a strong deviation from the spontaneous state, which then settled into repeated loops (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the three-dimensional projection shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Capturing 80% of the population variance generally required 4–8 embedding dimensions.
source: Capturing a significant proportion (80%) of the population variance generally required 4–8 embedding dimensions (Figure 2B), representing a dimension reduction by more than a factor of 10 compared to the number of neurons.
evidence: This is supported by the variance explained data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The dimension reduction achieved represents more than a factor of 10 compared to the number of neurons.
source: Capturing a significant proportion (80%) of the population variance generally required 4–8 embedding dimensions (Figure 2B), representing a dimension reduction by more than a factor of 10 compared to the number of neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison between 4-8 dimensions and 120-180 neurons.

claim: Almost all evoked population responses quickly reached a state of high recurrence within one oscillation period.
source: We found that almost all evoked population responses quickly reached a state of high recurrence, within one oscillation period (Figure 3A), and were thereafter dominated by recurrence, indicating they quickly reached and stayed on the manifold.
evidence: This is supported by the coalescence time data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Pairs of evoked population responses from the same preparation fell close to each other throughout.
source: Despite the inherent noise and limited duration of the recordings, this is exactly what we found: pairs of evoked population responses from the same preparation fell close to each other throughout (Figure 3C), well in excess of the expected agreement between random projections of the data onto the same embedding dimensions.
evidence: This is supported by the distance measurements shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The convergence to the same manifold exceeded the expected agreement between random projections.
source: Despite the inherent noise and limited duration of the recordings, this is exactly what we found: pairs of evoked population responses from the same preparation fell close to each other throughout (Figure 3C), well in excess of the expected agreement between random projections of the data onto the same embedding dimensions.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with control data in Figure 3C.

claim: The stimulation caused population responses within the same preparation to diverge far more than in either the spontaneous activity or after coalescing to the manifold.
source: We found that the stimulation caused population responses within the same preparation to diverge far more than in either the spontaneous activity or after coalescing to the manifold (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by the distance measurements across different states shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Pair-wise similarity is well-preserved across population responses in the same preparation.
source: We found that pair-wise similarity is indeed well-preserved across population responses in the same preparation (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: In most cases (90%), the population dynamics returned to a recurrent state after spontaneous perturbation.
source: In most cases (90%), the population dynamics returned to a recurrent state after the spontaneous perturbation (Figure 3H; Figure 3—figure supplement 2, panel B), consistent with the pertubation being caused by a transient effect on the population
evidence: This is supported by the perturbation analysis data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Of the perturbations that returned to a recurrent state, all but three clearly returned to the same manifold.
source: Of those that returned, all but three clearly returned to the same manifold (Figure 3I); for those three, the spontaneous perturbation appeared sufficient to move the population dynamics into a different periodic attractor (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, panel C).
evidence: This is supported by the recurrence analysis shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The evoked population responses had highly clustered maximum eigenvalues.
source: Doing so, we found that the evoked population responses had highly clustered maximum eigenvalues (Figure 4B,C), and thus highly similar underlying dynamics despite the apparent heterogeneity of spike-train patterns between them.
evidence: This is supported by the eigenvalue clustering shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: The evoked population responses have highly similar underlying dynamics despite the apparent heterogeneity of spike-train patterns.
source: Doing so, we found that the evoked population responses had highly clustered maximum eigenvalues (Figure 4B,C), and thus highly similar underlying dynamics despite the apparent heterogeneity of spike-train patterns between them.
evidence: This is an inference based on the eigenvalue clustering data.

claim: The dominance of negative complex eigenvalues implies the pedal ganglion network implements a contracting periodic orbit - a stable spiral attractor.
source: The dominance of negative complex eigenvalues implies the pedal ganglion network implements a contracting periodic orbit - it is a stable spiral attractor (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an inference from the eigenvalue analysis, supported by the visualization in Figure 4D.

claim: The linear model estimated a mean orbital period of around 10 s.
source: The linear model estimated a mean orbital period of around 10 s (Figure 4C), consistent with the directly-derived estimate from the recurrent points (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by the orbital period estimates shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The linear model's estimate of orbital period is consistent with the directly-derived estimate from the recurrent points.
source: The linear model estimated a mean orbital period of around 10 s (Figure 4C), consistent with the directly-derived estimate from the recurrent points (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a comparison between two different analytical approaches shown in Figures 4C and 2F.

claim: The population responses included all possible changes in periodic orbit: slowing, speeding up, and not changing.
source: We found that the population responses included all possible changes in periodic orbit: slowing, speeding up, and not changing (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the histogram of correlations shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There was no relationship between the contraction of the periodic orbit and its change in period.
source: As predicted there was no relationship between the contraction of the periodic orbit and its change in period (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by the lack of correlation shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In 3 of the 10 preparations, simultaneous recording of P10 nerve activity was achieved for all three evoked population responses.
source: In 3 of the 10 preparations we were able to simultaneously record activity from the P10 nerve that projects to the neck muscles (Xin et al., 1996) for all three evoked population responses.
evidence: This describes the subset of experiments with P10 recordings.

claim: The P10 nerve projects to the neck muscles.
source: In 3 of the 10 preparations we were able to simultaneously record activity from the P10 nerve that projects to the neck muscles (Xin et al., 1996) for all three evoked population responses.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior anatomical work.

claim: The model could accurately fit and forecast P10 activity from the low-dimensional trajectory in all nine population responses.
source: The model could accurately fit and forecast P10 activity from the low-dimensional trajectory in all nine population responses (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by the decoding results shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The successful decoding of future P10 activity was achieved despite needing only 3–5 embedding dimensions to account for 80% variance.
source: The successful decoding of future P10 activity was achieved despite needing only 3–5 embedding dimensions to account for 80% variance in the population activity for these nine recordings (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the dimensionality analysis in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Increasing the number of embedding dimensions to account for 90% variance did not improve the forecasts of P10 activity.
source: Increasing the number of embedding dimensions to account for 90% variance, at least doubling the number of embedding dimensions, did not improve the forecasts of P10 activity (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Every population response had a long-tailed distribution of participation.
source: Every population response had a long-tailed distribution of participation (Figure 7A), indicating that a minority of neurons dominated the dynamics of any given response.
evidence: This is supported by the participation distributions shown in Figure 7A.

claim: A minority of neurons dominated the dynamics of any given response.
source: Every population response had a long-tailed distribution of participation (Figure 7A), indicating that a minority of neurons dominated the dynamics of any given response.
evidence: This is an inference from the long-tailed distribution shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Many neurons with high participation in one population response showed low participation in another.
source: Nonetheless, these neurons were not fixed: many with high participation in one population response showed low participation in another (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This is supported by the participation change data shown in Figures 7B and 7C.

claim: Every preparation's pedal ganglion contained neurons whose change in participation between responses well-exceeded that predicted by the noise model.
source: Every preparation's pedal ganglion contained neurons whose change in participation between responses well-exceeded that predicted by the noise model (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by the strongly variable neuron analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The distance between a pair of population responses did not correlate with the total change in neuron participation between the two responses.
source: We found that the distance between a pair of population responses did not correlate with either the total change in neuron participation between the two responses (Figure 7G) or the distance between their participation distributions (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is supported by the lack of correlation shown in Figure 7G.

claim: The distance between a pair of population responses did not correlate with the distance between their participation distributions.
source: We found that the distance between a pair of population responses did not correlate with either the total change in neuron participation between the two responses (Figure 7G) or the distance between their participation distributions (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is supported by the lack of correlation shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Neurons with strong participation across the three evoked population responses were robustly located in the caudo-lateral quadrant of the ganglion.
source: We found that neurons with strong participation across the three evoked population responses were robustly located in the caudo-lateral quadrant of the ganglion (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the spatial maps shown in Figures 8A and 8B.

claim: Neurons with highly variable participation between population responses were found in the caudo-lateral quadrants of both ganglia.
source: Neurons with highly variable participation between population responses (Figure 8C,D) were similarly found in the caudo-lateral quadrants of both ganglia.
evidence: This is supported by the spatial maps shown in Figures 8C and 8D.

claim: The low-dimensional trajectory of the periodic attractor appears to directly encode muscle commands for movement.
source: Thus, the low dimensional trajectory of the periodic attractor appears to directly encode muscle commands for movement.
evidence: This is an inference based on the successful decoding of P10 activity from the low-dimensional trajectory.

claim: Only the low-dimensional dynamics for movement control, and not the high-dimensional population activity, are consistent within and between nervous systems.
source: From these results, we propose that only the low-dimensional dynamics for movement control, and not the high-dimensional population activity, are consistent within and between nervous systems.
evidence: This is a synthesis claim based on the findings of consistent low-dimensional dynamics despite variable high-dimensional activity.

claim: The pedal ganglion's population-wide activity arises from a low-dimensional spiral attractor.
source: By imaging Aplysia's pedal ganglion during fictive locomotion, here we show that its population-wide activity arises from a low-dimensional spiral attractor.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple analyses throughout the manuscript.

claim: Evoking locomotion moved the population into a low-dimensional, periodic, decaying orbit.
source: Evoking locomotion moved the population into a low-dimensional, periodic, decaying orbit - a spiral - in which it behaved as a true attractor, converging to the same orbit when evoked, and returning to that orbit after transient perturbation.
evidence: This summarizes the key experimental findings about the spiral attractor properties.

claim: The low-dimensional orbit behaved as a true attractor, converging to the same orbit when evoked.
source: Evoking locomotion moved the population into a low-dimensional, periodic, decaying orbit - a spiral - in which it behaved as a true attractor, converging to the same orbit when evoked, and returning to that orbit after transient perturbation.
evidence: This is supported by the convergence analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The low-dimensional orbit returned to the same trajectory after transient perturbation.
source: Evoking locomotion moved the population into a low-dimensional, periodic, decaying orbit - a spiral - in which it behaved as a true attractor, converging to the same orbit when evoked, and returning to that orbit after transient perturbation.
evidence: This is supported by the perturbation analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The same attractor was found in every preparation.
source: We found the same attractor in every preparation, and could predict motor output directly from its orbit, yet individual neurons' participation changed across consecutive locomotion bouts.
evidence: This is supported by the eigenvalue clustering across preparations shown in Figure 4.

claim: Motor output can be predicted directly from the attractor's orbit.
source: We found the same attractor in every preparation, and could predict motor output directly from its orbit, yet individual neurons' participation changed across consecutive locomotion bouts.
evidence: This is supported by the P10 decoding results shown in Figure 6.

claim: Individual neurons' participation changed across consecutive locomotion bouts.
source: We found the same attractor in every preparation, and could predict motor output directly from its orbit, yet individual neurons' participation changed across consecutive locomotion bouts.
evidence: This is supported by the participation variability analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Movement arises from the mass action of neuron populations.
source: Movement arises from the mass action of neuron populations (Georgopoulos et al., 1986; Getting, 1989; Ahrens et al., 2012; Portugues et al., 2014; Yuste, 2015; Petersen and Berg, 2016).
evidence: This is a general principle supported by multiple citations.

claim: Individual neuron activity can correlate with specific aspects of movement.
source: While individual neuron activity can correlate with specific aspects of movement (Chestek et al., 2007; Hatsopoulos et al., 2007; Churchland et al., 2010, 2012), the embedded low dimensional signals in population recordings (Briggman et al., 2005; Levi et al., 2005; Kato et al., 2015) and the intermittent participation of individual neurons across repeated movements in both vertebrates (Carmena et al., 2005; Huber et al., 2012) and invertebrates (Hill et al., 2010, 2015) together suggest that only the collective population activity, and not specifics of single neuron firing, are key to movement control.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Individual neurons show intermittent participation across repeated movements in vertebrates.
source: While individual neuron activity can correlate with specific aspects of movement (Chestek et al., 2007; Hatsopoulos et al., 2007; Churchland et al., 2010, 2012), the embedded low dimensional signals in population recordings (Briggman et al., 2005; Levi et al., 2005; Kato et al., 2015) and the intermittent participation of individual neurons across repeated movements in both vertebrates (Carmena et al., 2005; Huber et al., 2012) and invertebrates (Hill et al., 2010, 2015) together suggest that only the collective population activity, and not specifics of single neuron firing, are key to movement control.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on vertebrates.

claim: Individual neurons show intermittent participation across repeated movements in invertebrates.
source: While individual neuron activity can correlate with specific aspects of movement (Chestek et al., 2007; Hatsopoulos et al., 2007; Churchland et al., 2010, 2012), the embedded low dimensional signals in population recordings (Briggman et al., 2005; Levi et al., 2005; Kato et al., 2015) and the intermittent participation of individual neurons across repeated movements in both vertebrates (Carmena et al., 2005; Huber et al., 2012) and invertebrates (Hill et al., 2010, 2015) together suggest that only the collective population activity, and not specifics of single neuron firing, are key to movement control.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on invertebrates.

claim: Only the collective population activity, and not specifics of single neuron firing, are key to movement control.
source: While individual neuron activity can correlate with specific aspects of movement (Chestek et al., 2007; Hatsopoulos et al., 2007; Churchland et al., 2010, 2012), the embedded low dimensional signals in population recordings (Briggman et al., 2005; Levi et al., 2005; Kato et al., 2015) and the intermittent participation of individual neurons across repeated movements in both vertebrates (Carmena et al., 2005; Huber et al., 2012) and invertebrates (Hill et al., 2010, 2015) together suggest that only the collective population activity, and not specifics of single neuron firing, are key to movement control.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited literature and the authors' interpretation.

claim: A strong tail stimulus typically elicits a two-part escape behavior in intact Aplysia consisting of several cycles of vigorous arching gallop followed by several minutes of rhythmic crawl.
source: We know the pedal ganglion contains a mix of interneurons and motorneurons (Fredman and Jahan-Parwar, 1980), and that the motorneurons are not synaptically coupled (Hening et al., 1979), suggesting they read-out (and potentially feedback to) the dynamics of an interneuron network.
evidence: This is supported by citations describing the natural behavior.

claim: The pedal ganglion contains a mix of interneurons and motorneurons.
source: We know the pedal ganglion contains a mix of interneurons and motorneurons (Fredman and Jahan-Parwar, 1980), and that the motorneurons are not synaptically coupled (Hening et al., 1979), suggesting they read-out (and potentially feedback to) the dynamics of an interneuron network.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior anatomical work.

claim: The motorneurons in the pedal ganglion are not synaptically coupled.
source: We know the pedal ganglion contains a mix of interneurons and motorneurons (Fredman and Jahan-Parwar, 1980), and that the motorneurons are not synaptically coupled (Hening et al., 1979), suggesting they read-out (and potentially feedback to) the dynamics of an interneuron network.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior physiological work.

claim: The motorneurons read-out and potentially feedback to the dynamics of an interneuron network.
source: We know the pedal ganglion contains a mix of interneurons and motorneurons (Fredman and Jahan-Parwar, 1980), and that the motorneurons are not synaptically coupled (Hening et al., 1979), suggesting they read-out (and potentially feedback to) the dynamics of an interneuron network.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical and physiological properties cited.

claim: The caudo-lateral region of the pedal ganglion contains neural ensembles that generate cyclical packet of neural activity in phase with P10 nerve activity.
source: Encouragingly, from a different data-set we previously described this region as containing neural ensembles that generated a cyclical packet of neural activity, which moved in phase with activity from the neck-projecting P10 nerve (Bruno et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: The pattern generator for locomotion is predominantly located in the caudo-lateral network of the pedal ganglion.
source: Consequently, both those data and our new data support our hypothesis that the pattern generator for locomotion is predominantly located in the caudo-lateral network.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by both prior work and the current spatial mapping data.

claim: The orbital period of the attractor determines the period of the rhythmic gallop.
source: In this hypothesis, the orbital period of the attractor determines the period of the rhythmic gallop – the sequential activity of the neurons in each orbit thus driving the sequential contraction of the muscles driving the escape gallop (Bruno et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: The amplitude of the orbital period could determine the strength of muscle contraction during the escape gallop.
source: Further, the amplitude of the orbital period, corresponding to the spike rate of the neural population, could determine the strength of muscle contraction during the escape gallop, allowing control of the physical distance covered by each arching movement.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: The contraction rate of the attractor determines the duration of the escape.
source: Finally, the contraction rate of the attractor determines the duration of the escape: the faster the contraction rate, the shorter the escape gallop's duration.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Systemic injection of serotonin increases gallop duration.
source: For example, the reported increase in gallop duration by systemic injection of serotonin (Marinesco et al., 2004) should correlate with a decreased contraction rate of the attractor.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on serotonin effects.

claim: A spiral attractor is potentially a general solution to the problem of how to generate a finite rhythmic behaviour.
source: Indeed, a spiral attractor is potentially a general solution to the problem of how to generate a finite rhythmic behaviour.
evidence: This is a speculative generalization based on the findings.

claim: The variable participation of neurons supports the hypothesis that periodic activity is an emergent property of the network.
source: These results suggest that the pedal ganglion's pattern generator is not driven by neurons that are endogenous oscillators, as they would be expected to participate equally in every response. Rather, this variation supports the hypothesis that the periodic activity is an emergent property of the network.
evidence: This is an inference based on the participation variability data.

claim: Having variably participating neurons may make the pedal ganglion's ability to generate locomotion robust to the loss of neurons.
source: One possibility is that, by not relying on any core set of neurons to generate rhythmic activity, the pedal ganglion's ability to generate locomotion is robust to the loss of neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed variability.

claim: There may be sloppiness in the pedal ganglion network such that many possible configurations of neurons can realize the spiral attractor.
source: A related possibility is that there is 'sloppiness' (Panas et al., 2015) in the pedal ganglion network, such that there are many possible configurations of neurons and their connections able to realise the spiral attractor that drives locomotion (Marder et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation citing the concept of sloppiness from prior work.

claim: The pedal ganglion network supports at least two stable states: spontaneous activity and the stable-spiral attractor.
source: Our data further suggest that the pedal ganglion network supports at least two stable states, the spontaneous activity and the stable-spiral attractor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of distinct dynamical states.

claim: Reaching the stable-spiral attractor from spontaneous activity required long-duration, high-voltage pedal nerve stimulation.
source: Reaching the stable-spiral attractor from the spontaneous activity required long-duration, high-voltage pedal nerve stimulation (Figure 1; Bruno et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions needed to evoke the attractor state.

claim: The spontaneous state's basin of attraction is large.
source: In dynamical systems terms, this suggests that the spontaneous state's basin of attraction is large: most perturbations return to that state, and it takes a large perturbation to move into a different basin of attraction.
evidence: This is an inference from dynamical systems theory applied to the experimental observations.

claim: Escape galloping is dramatically extended by systemic injection of serotonin alongside tail stimulation.
source: One possibility in the pedal ganglion is that serotonin alters the effective connections between neurons: escape galloping is both dramatically extended by systemic injection of serotonin alongside tail stimulation (Marinesco et al., 2004), and evoked by stimulating serotonergic command neurons CC9/CC10 in the cerebral ganglion (Jing et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on serotonin effects.

claim: Escape galloping is evoked by stimulating serotonergic command neurons CC9/CC10 in the cerebral ganglion.
source: One possibility in the pedal ganglion is that serotonin alters the effective connections between neurons: escape galloping is both dramatically extended by systemic injection of serotonin alongside tail stimulation (Marinesco et al., 2004), and evoked by stimulating serotonergic command neurons CC9/CC10 in the cerebral ganglion (Jing et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on command neurons.

claim: The long-lasting crawl that follows the escape gallop is slower and omits the periodic arching of the body.
source: The long-lasting crawl that follows the escape gallop is slower and omits the periodic arching of the body (Flinn et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior behavioral work.

claim: Three perturbations of the attractor activity were suggestive of a transition to a different, slower periodic orbit.
source: We saw three perturbations of the attractor activity that were suggestive of a transition to a different, slower periodic orbit (e.g. panel C in Figure 3—figure supplement 2), consistent with a transition from galloping to crawling.
evidence: This is an observation from the data with an interpretation about behavioral transitions.

claim: Crawling is the animal's normal mode of exploration.
source: Such crawling is also the animal's normal mode of exploration (Leonard and Lukowiak, 1986), and so the 'crawling' attractor must be reachable from the spontaneous state too.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior behavioral work.

claim: Aplysia's exploratory head-wave is controlled by motorneurons in the pedal ganglion.
source: Aplysia's exploratory head-wave, moving its head side-to-side presumably to allow its tentacles and other head sensory organs to sample the environment (Leonard and Lukowiak, 1986), is also controlled by motorneurons in the pedal ganglion (Kuenzi and Carew, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on head-wave behavior.

claim: Multi-functional networks have been described in Aplysia's abdominal ganglion.
source: Previous studies of the Aplysia's abdominal ganglion (Wu et al., 1994), the leech segmental ganglion (Briggman and Kristan, 2006), and the crustacean stomatogastric ganglion (reviewed in Marder and Bucher, 2007) have described multi-functional networks in which the same neurons are active in different motor behaviours.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Multi-functional networks have been described in the leech segmental ganglion.
source: Previous studies of the Aplysia's abdominal ganglion (Wu et al., 1994), the leech segmental ganglion (Briggman and Kristan, 2006), and the crustacean stomatogastric ganglion (reviewed in Marder and Bucher, 2007) have described multi-functional networks in which the same neurons are active in different motor behaviours.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Multi-functional networks have been described in the crustacean stomatogastric ganglion.
source: Previous studies of the Aplysia's abdominal ganglion (Wu et al., 1994), the leech segmental ganglion (Briggman and Kristan, 2006), and the crustacean stomatogastric ganglion (reviewed in Marder and Bucher, 2007) have described multi-functional networks in which the same neurons are active in different motor behaviours.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Multi-function in neural networks may be due to neurons participating in different attractors realized by the same network.
source: Our work here is consistent with the hypothesis that such multi-function is due to the neurons participating in different attractors realised by same network (Briggman and Kristan, 2008).
evidence: This is a hypothesis consistent with the current findings and cited prior work.

claim: Imaging used the fast voltage sensitive absorbance dye RH-155.
source: Imaging of neural activity used the fast voltage sensitive absorbance dye RH-155 (Anaspec), and a 464-element photodiode array (NeuroPDA-III, RedShirtImaging) sampled at 1600 Hz.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used.

claim: A 464-element photodiode array was used for imaging, sampled at 1600 Hz.
source: Imaging of neural activity used the fast voltage sensitive absorbance dye RH-155 (Anaspec), and a 464-element photodiode array (NeuroPDA-III, RedShirtImaging) sampled at 1600 Hz.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used.

claim: Rhythmic locomotion motor programs were elicited using 8V 5 ms monophasic pulses delivered at 20 Hz for 2.5 s via suction electrode to pedal nerve 9.
source: Rhythmic locomotion motor programs were elicited using 8V 5 ms monophasic pulses delivered at 20 Hz for 2.5 s via suction electrode to pedal nerve 9.
evidence: This describes the experimental stimulation protocol.
